Prologue.

How mistaken our ancestors had been, in their understanding of created things, both Greeks and Latins: this is very clear from their own writings. From which it is evident how ridiculous were the fables they invented about the sun, and the moon, and some of the stars: and about water, earth, fire, and air: and about other creatures: and what is worse, they attributed divinity to them: and worshipped, offered sacrifices to, and honored them as gods. This came about in part through the blindness into which we fell because of original sin: and in part through the malice and inveterate hatred of our adversary, Satan: who always strives to cast us down to vile, ridiculous, and most blameworthy things. Well, if this happened, as we know, among people of such discretion and self-regard, there is no reason for anyone to marvel that similar things are found among this people [the Indians]: so simple and so easy to deceive. It is therefore fitting that they be cured of their blindness, both by means of preachers and of confessors: and so there are set down in the present book some of the fables, no less foolish than frivolous, that their ancestors left them: about the sun, the moon, and the stars: and about the elements, and things composed of elements. At the end of the book is given the manner of counting the years: and of the Jubilee year, which came every fifty-two years: and of the notable ceremonies that they performed then.

To the Reader.

The reader will have reason to be displeased in reading this seventh book, and much more so if he understands the Indian language together with the Spanish: because in the Spanish the language is very low, and the subject matter treated in this seventh book is dealt with very basely. This is because the natives themselves gave the account of the things treated in this book in a very base manner, according to how they understand them: and in low language. And thus it was translated into the Spanish language in a low style, and with a low degree of understanding: intending only to know and to write down what they themselves understood on this subject, of astrology and natural philosophy — which is very little and very base. There is another thing in the language that will also displease whoever understands it: that for one thing there go many synonyms: and one way of saying something, or one sentence, is expressed in many different ways: this was done on purpose, in order to know and write down all the words for each thing, and all the ways of expressing each sentence: and this applies not only to this book but to the whole work. Farewell.

Seventh Book, concerning Astrology.                               fol. 1.

¶ The seventh book treats
of the sun, and of the moon, and
the stars, and of the year of the
Jubilee.
Chapter one, concerning the sun.

The sun has the property of
shining, and of giving light,
and of casting rays from itself.
It is hot, and it scorches: it
makes one sweat, in order to
make dark and fragrant the
body and the face of a person.

They held a feast for the sun
once each year, on the sign
called "Nahui Ollin" (Four
Movement): and before the
feast they fasted for four days,
as a vigil for the feast. And in
this feast of the sun they offered
incense and the blood of sheep
four times: once at sunrise,
again at midday, and at the
hour of vespers, and when it
set. And when it rose in the
morning, they would say, "now
the sun begins its work—
whatever it may be, whatever
will happen this day." And at
sunset they would say, "the sun
has finished its work, or its
task." At times, when the sun
rises, it appears...

¶ Here begins the seventh book,

Chapter one, which speaks of

¶ The Sun: "Eagle that Rises,"
"Turquoise Prince," "Deity."
It shines, it gives light, it
radiates: it is hot, it burns
people, it scorches, it blinds;
it darkens faces, it blackens,
it browns, it chars the face.
¶ Every two hundred days,
after one hundred and sixty
(days), its feast day would
arrive; its festival was
celebrated, its feast was held
with reverence: they rejoiced,
for its day sign was called
"Nahui Ollin." And before its
feast day arrived, first, for
four days, there was fasting.
And when the day of its feast
came, when it newly appeared,
when it emerged, when it shone
forth, there was incense-offering,
there was warming of fires,
there was bloodletting. This was
done four times in a single day:
at dawn, and at midday for the
sun, and also when it began to
decline, when it began to sink;
and also when it entered, when
it set, when it hid itself. And
at dawn it was said: "now it
will begin its task, now the sun
will perform its office: however
it may turn out..."

[Illustration: two painted suns with faces]

When the sun is eclipsed, it turns reddish, as though it were entirely bleeding, or the sun becomes disturbed, or it shakes, or churns, and grows very yellow. When the people see this happen, they are immediately thrown into turmoil, and great fear seizes them. Then the women weep aloud, and the men shout, striking their mouths with their hands. Everywhere great cries, shouts, and wailing arose. Then they went looking for men with white hair and white faces, and sacrificed them to the sun. They also sacrificed captives, and anointed [the sun] with blood from the ears; and likewise they pierced their ears with maguey thorns and passed reeds, or something similar, through the holes the thorns had made. Then, throughout all the temples, they sang and played instruments, making a great noise. And they said that if the eclipse were to be complete...

...the day. And at night it was said: it has labored, the sun has grown weary. Thus it would appear — sometimes strong, red, intensely colored. And sometimes it would turn only pale, only whitish, only yellowish, because of the mist, the haze, or else because of dust or spotted darkness spreading over its face.

The Eating of the Sun.

When this happens and it turns red and spreads out, no longer is there order, no longer is there calm; everything is thrown into confusion. It grows very yellow; then there is a crackling sound, the people cry out: there is commotion, there is uproar, there is fear, there is weeping; shouting rises among the common people. There is biting of lips, there is gaping of mouths, there is shouting, there is calling out, people cry aloud. Night spreads over everything. People turn pale with terror; there is killing of captives, there is bloodletting, there is piercing of ears. And in the ruler's palace there is singing, there is commotion, there is disturbance. Thus it was said: if the eating of the sun should be completed, utter darkness would fall, and the Tzitzimime would descend to devour mankind.

And natural philosophy

...be the sun, it will shine no more,
perpetual darkness will set in,
and the demons will descend, they will come
to eat us.
¶ Second chapter, on the moon.

When the moon is newly
born, it appears like a thin thread
of fine wire that gives no light at all;
little by little it goes on growing.
At fifteen days it is full, and
when it is already full, it rises in
the east, at the setting of the sun: it appears
like a great millwheel,
very round and very
red. And as it goes rising,
it turns white, and shines
more brightly: it looks like a rabbit
in its midst. And if there are no
clouds, it shines almost like
the sun, almost as if it were day. And after
it has been completely full,
little by little it begins to wane,
until it becomes as it was
when it began. They say then
that the moon is dying, that it
darkens greatly: this is when
it rises already with the dawn, at the time
of conjunction: they say then
that the moon is dead.

¶ Here begins the second chapter, which speaks
of: the moon.

¶ The moon, Tecuciztecatl.

When it first
newly appears, it comes forth small and curved: like a
small carrying-yoke, a little carrying-hook, it does not
yet give light: only thus it goes along,
growing round, becoming circular,
becoming rounded like a wheel. In fifteen days it
becomes fully round: becomes wheel-like, it
reaches its fullness, it becomes strong. And when
it has become perfectly circular, has become fully round, then
it truly appears: thus it comes forth, there
where the sun rises: when
it begins to grow dim, it is like a griddle,
very large: fully rounded,
circular: like something red, very
red, deeply red. And then,
when it begins to decline a little, when it
goes down and rises again, it turns white: it is said it now looks,
it now gives light, the moon now
shines: pale, very white, thus
it is seen: thus it appears, like a rabbit
lying crouched within it: if there are no
clouds, if it is not misty, if mist does not gather:
thus it gives light, thus dawn comes, they say
that this is a complete day, true full moonlight:
it remains shining brightly through the night. And
when it has fully reached,
fully attained its shining: for that many days, thus it
grows, becomes round: only thus it continues on,

The fable of the rabbit that is in the moon is this one. They say that the gods mocked the moon, and struck it with a rabbit in the face, and the rabbit left it marked on the face; and with this they darkened its face, as if with a bruise. After this, it went out to light the world. They say that before there was day in the world, the gods gathered together in that place called Teotihuacan — which is the town of San Juan, between Chiconauhtlan and the tombs — and said to one another, "Gods, who shall take charge of lighting the world?" Then, in answer to these words, a god who was called Tecuciztecatl replied and said, "I take upon myself the charge of lighting the world." Then again the gods spoke and said, "Who shall be the other one?" Then they looked at one another, and discussed among themselves who the other would be; and none of them dared to offer himself,

Again it grows small, it goes on growing small; again thus it happens, newly it appears when it rises anew: only when it disappears do they say the moon has died; when it is large, it sleeps; when it is sleeping, it goes on dawning, it dawns far off, until it comes forth. And when it has completely disappeared, it is said: the moon has died.

¶ Here is the account of why it is said that something like a little rabbit lies spread upon the face of the moon. It is said that thereby it was disgraced, thereby it was struck in the face, thereby its face was scratched, thereby it was ruined, thereby the gods wounded it, when afterward it came forth and appeared. It is said that in the time of darkness, before there was sunlight, before there was dawn, the gods gathered together, they took counsel among themselves there at Teotihuacan, and they said, they declared to one another: "Come here, O gods; who will take the burden, who will bear the task of giving light, of bringing the dawn?" And then he spoke up, he stood forth there — Tecuciztecatl — and said: "O gods, I shall be the one." Again the gods said: "Who else?" Then they looked one upon another, they showed themselves to each other, they discussed how it would be, who it would be, who they would become.

There was one of the gods of whom no account was made, and who was covered with sores: he did not speak, but only listened to what the other gods were saying. The other gods spoke to him, and said to him: "You be the one to give light, O sore-covered one." And he, of good will, obeyed what they had ordered him, and replied: "I receive as a favor what you have commanded me; so be it." And then the two of them began to do penance, for four days.

And then they lit a fire on the hearth, which had been made in a rock (which they now call teotexcalli). The god called Tecuciztecatl offered only precious things: instead of branches, he offered rich feathers called quetzalli; instead of balls of hay, he offered balls of gold; instead of maguey thorns, he offered thorns made of precious stones; and instead of blood-stained thorns, he offered thorns made of red coral; and the copal incense he offered was of the finest kind. And the sore-covered one, who was called Nanahuatzin, instead of branches offered green reeds tied in bundles of three, all of which together came to nine; and he offered balls of hay and maguey thorns, and stained them with his own blood: and instead...

No one dared to put himself forward for that task, for everyone trembled with fear and grew faint of heart. But there was one who did not hold back — a certain man named Nanahuatzin — he remained there humbly with the others while it was being discussed. Then they called to him, the gods said to him: "You shall be the one, O Nanahuatzin." At once he gladly accepted the word spoken to him, saying: "This is good; you have done me a kindness." Then they began their penance: they both remained in it for four days, he and Tecuciztecatl. And at that time also a fire was kindled; it burned there in the hearth, which they named teotexcalli (the divine hearth). And this Tecuciztecatl, in his penance, offered all precious things: his pine-branch offerings were of quetzal feathers, his hay-balls were of gold, his thorns were of jade, and his blood-offerings were of coral; and his copal was true copal. But Nanahuatzin's pine branches were only of green reed cane, all tied together in bundles of three, nine in total; his hay-balls were merely of rough dry grass, and his thorns were simply of maguey spines; and with these he drew his own blood very well...

...of copal, offered the scabs of the pustules [of the diseased god]. For each of these two, a tower was built like a mountain, upon these same mountains they did penance for four nights (these mountains are now called tzaqualli, and both are located near the town of San Juan, which is called Teotihuacan). When the four nights of their penance ended, they then threw away, in that place, their beds and all the other things with which they had done penance. This happened at the end, or close, of their penance, when the following night was about to begin — at midnight they were to start performing their duties. And a little before midnight, they were given their adornments. To the one called Tecuciztecatl they gave a plume called aztacomitl, and a jacket of fine linen; and the pustuled one, called Nanahuatzin, had his head covered with paper called amatzontli, and they put upon him a stole of paper and a loincloth of paper. And when midnight arrived, all the gods arranged themselves around the hearth called teotexcalli; in this place the fire burned for four days. The said gods arranged themselves in two rows: some on one side of the fire, others on the other side. Then the two aforementioned ones placed themselves before the fire, their faces turned toward it, in the middle of the two rows...

[Nahuatl, parallel text:] ...his blood; and his copal, for it was that which caused the sickness [pustules]. The two of them together, each one, became a mountain: there they did penance for four nights, it is said; now [these are called] the twin mounds, the mound of the Sun and the mound of the Moon. And when the four nights of penance were completed, then they cast away and scattered all that with which they had done penance. This happened when night was falling, when they were to keep vigil and do service. And when midnight arrived, then they were given their array, they were adorned, they were arrayed: to Tecuciztecatl they gave the heron-feather headdress, the striped, rounded one, and the sleeveless jacket. But to Nanahuatzin they gave only paper, with which they bound him: they tied on him his paper headdress, called amatzontli, and his paper stole, and his paper breechcloth. And when this was done, and midnight had fully come, all the gods arranged themselves in a circle around the hearth, called teotexcalli, where for four days the fire had burned; on either side they ranged themselves, and in the middle they placed and stood the two, who are called Tecuciz[tecatl]...

...cles, of the gods: who were all standing. And then the gods spoke, and said to Tecuciztecatl: "Now then, Tecuciztecatl, enter into the fire." And he then rushed to throw himself into the fire. And as the fire was great, and was burning very fiercely: when he felt the great heat of the fire, he grew afraid, and did not dare to throw himself into the fire; he drew back. Again he turned to throw himself into the fire, gathering his strength, and approaching he stopped, not daring to throw himself in. But feeling the great heat, he stopped again, not daring to throw himself in. Four times he tried, but he never dared to throw himself in. It had been ordained that he should not try more than four times. After he had tried four times, the gods then spoke to Nanahuatzin, and said to him: "Now then, Nanahuatzin, you try." And as the gods had spoken to him, he forced himself, and closing his eyes, he rushed forward and threw himself into the fire. And then he began to crackle and sizzle in the fire, like one being roasted. And when Tecuciztecatl saw that he had thrown himself into the fire and was burning, he too rushed forward and threw himself into the fire. And it is said that then an eagle entered the fire, and also...

...tecatl and Nanahuatzin met each other, they stood facing one another at the hearth. And then the gods spoke, they said to Tecuciztecatl: "O valiant Tecuciztecatl, fall! Throw yourself into the fire!" Then he went to throw himself into the fire. But the heat that reached him was unbearable, intolerable, unendurable: for the hearth-fire had blazed up greatly, had grown immense, the fire had settled firmly in place. Thus he only frightened himself, he went and stood looking at it, he turned back, he fled. Then once more he went to try to reach it, gathering all his strength, thus he hurled himself toward the fire: but he could not bring himself to dare it; when again he drew near the heat, he only turned back, he fled, he did not accomplish it. Four times — four times he did thus, as was required — but he could not throw himself into the fire; for that was the limit set, the four times. And when the four attempts were finished, then he cried out to Nanahuatzin; the gods spoke to him. "Now you..."

And they say "eagle" first, because the eagle entered the fire first: and they say afterward "ocelotl" (tiger), because the tiger entered the fire after the eagle. This table, set above, is the count of the years, and it is a very
ancient thing. They say that its inventor was Quetzalcoatl: it
proceeds in this manner: they begin from the East, which is where
the reeds are; and according to others, from the south, where the
rabbit is, and they say "ce acatl" (one reed): and from there they
go to the North, where the flint is, and they say "ome tecpatl"
(two flint): then they go to the West, where the house is, and
there they say "yei calli" (three house): and then they go to the
southwest, which is where the rabbit is, and they say "nahui
tochtli" (four rabbit): and then they return to the East, and they
say "macuilli acatl" (five reed). And thus they go making four
turns, until they reach thirteen, which end where they began: and
then they return to one, saying "ce tecpatl" (one flint). In this
manner, going around, they give thirteen years to each one of the
characters, or to each one of the four parts of the world. And then
fifty-two years are completed, which is a bundle of years: where
the Jubilee is celebrated, and new fire is drawn, in the manner set
forth above: then they begin counting again as from the start. It
should be noted that there is much discrepancy in various places
regarding the beginning of the year: in some places they told me
that it began on such-and-such a day of January: in others, that it
was the first of February: in others, that it was such-and-such a
day of March. In Tlatelolco I gathered many old men, the most
skilled that I could find, and together with the most able of the
students of the college, this matter was debated for many days;
and all of them concluded that the year began on the second day
of February.
